filename: Distilling Machine Learning’s Added Value_ Pareto Fronts in Atmospheric Applications.pdf
title: Distilling Machine Learning’s Added Value: Pareto Fronts in Atmospheric Applications
parameterization_target: Cloud cover, shortwave heating rate, and tropical precipitation rate
code_availability: Scripts and reduced data to reproduce figures: https://github.com/tbeucler/2024_Pareto_Distillation archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13217736. Cloud cover analysis and schemes: https://github.com/EyringMLClimateGroup/grundner23james_EquationDiscovery_CloudCover archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8220333. Radiative transfer code: ml4rt v4.0.1 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13160776 and https://github.com/thunderhoser/ml4rt. Precipitation code: https://github.com/Sshamekh/Precip-org.
testbed_rationale: The datasets and code for cloud cover parameterization, radiative transfer emulation, and convective precipitation parameterization are publicly accessible on Zenodo and GitHub, providing direct benchmarks for Pareto-optimal atmospheric ML models.
pain_points: Full coarse-grained DYAMOND simulation output is multi-terabyte in size and hosted on HPC (DKRZ), requiring scripts to reconstruct from source files.

Non-local vertical connectivity or high-resolution spatial processing increases model complexity and computational footprint significantly compared to simpler distilled equations or recurrent architectures.
Temporal memory can partially compensate for the loss of subgrid convective organization in parameterizations, but error accumulation in coupled/online settings remains an open question.
extraction_notes: The paper provides three distinct case studies to illustrate Pareto-optimal model hierarchies for atmospheric processes: cloud cover parameterization (distilled via symbolic regression), shortwave radiative transfer emulation (distilled via bidirectional RNN), and tropical convective precipitation (distilled via temporal memory models).
